title: The ladder of joy
hookLine: the Taittiriya multiplies joy a hundredfold, rung after rung, then hands every rung to the one free of desire: the choice Nachiketa made at Death's door
carry: joy grows as wanting falls away
tomorrow: Bhrigu asks his father Varuna to teach him Brahman
last: BRAHMAN IS BRAHMAN IS BEYOND WORDS; NAMES ONLY POINT; NAMES ONLY POINT.

cards: A boy named Nachiketa once waited three days at the house of Death.

In the Katha Upanishad, Yama, the lord of death, offers him anything if he'll drop his question: long-lived sons, horses, gold, wide lands, a long life, lovely companions with music. Nachiketa says: keep them.
They don't last. Today the Taittiriya shows the math behind that answer. It takes the best life a human being could have, gives it one unit of joy, and starts multiplying.

teach.h: ONE UNIT: THE BEST HUMAN LIFE.
teach.b: Section eight is called, in later tradition, the inquiry into bliss. Here's the opening unit. Take a young man, good, well-read, quick, steady and strong, and suppose the whole earth, full of its wealth, belonged to him.
That is one measure of human bliss.

teach.h: TIMES A HUNDRED, RUNG AFTER RUNG.
teach.b: Now multiply it by a hundred. That's one bliss of the gandharvas, the heavenly musicians. A hundred of those, and you reach the divine gandharvas.
A hundred of those, the ancestors in their long-lasting world. Then the gods born in heaven. Then the gods who rose there by their deeds.
Then the gods. Then Indra, their king. Then Brihaspati, the gods' teacher.
Then Prajapati, the lord of creatures. And a hundred of his, the bliss of Brahman. But here's the line the passage turns on.

teach.h: AT EVERY RUNG: THE ONE WITHOUT DESIRE.
teach.b: At every rung above the first, the text adds: and so too for the one who knows the Veda and is not struck by desire. Shrotriya, akamahata.

teach.h: JOY GROWS AS WANTING FALLS AWAY.
teach.b: So the one who isn't gripped by wanting already has the bliss of the musicians, the gods, Indra, Prajapati.

The ladder doesn't have to be climbed. That's Nachiketa's choice, explained. And it's a teaching that runs all through Hindu life: joy doesn't come from adding things; it shows up as the grip of desire loosens.

Hindus practice it in small, ordinary ways, like a vrat, a vow to give something up for a day. And the very next section brings back yesterday's verse: the one who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing.

how: Vedanta teachers often read the ananda-mimamsa of Taittiriya 2.8 aloud and explain it as a lesson that joy grows as desire falls away, not as possessions grow.

o: a debate over who is happiest at court
the inquiry into bliss, measured rung by rung
a hymn of thanks for a good harvest

games.q: the ladder of bliss — tap the pairs.
p: a young man who owns the whole earth
a hundred times the one below

s: the text says only the gods can reach the highest bliss
at every rung it adds: so too for the learned one untouched by desire.
each rung of the ladder is a hundred times the one before
a hundred human blisses make one bliss of the gandharvas, and so on up.
the opening unit is the bliss of a beggar
it's a young man, good, learned and strong, who owns the whole earth.

games.q: you could own the whole earth and every treasure in it. the Taittiriya says someone else already has a hundred times that joy and more. who?
o: the learned one untouched by desire.
games.why: at every rung, the text says the same bliss belongs to the shrotriya, akamahata: the one who knows the Veda and is not struck by desire.

practice: A vrat can be as small as one breath. Notice one want that's present right now, a snack, a message you're waiting for, wanting this to be over, and without scolding it, name it softly and set it down for the length of one breath.
Then see if there's another, and set that one down too; between the wants, there may be a moment that needs nothing added. If you pray, you can offer each want as you set it down.

wordCard.voice: Ananda-mimamsa, the inquiry into bliss. Taittiriya 2.8: human joy multiplied by a hundred, rung after rung, up to Brahman, and the same bliss, at every rung, for the one untouched by desire.

orig.note: Sanskrit ānanda-mīmāṃsā, the inquiry into bliss: the traditional name for Taittiriya 2.8.

carryVoice: Your line: joy grows as wanting falls away. Like Nachiketa, you can say: keep it. Day three hundred ninety-five, done.
